headline_marked: [[Google Wallet gives kids tap-to-pay freedom]] with new parental controls and secure balances
headline: Google Wallet gives kids tap-to-pay freedom with new parental controls and secure balances
summary: Parents can now set up secure balances for children and teens on Google Wallet, allowing them to use Google Pay for tap-to-pay. This feature includes real-time transaction tracking and spending limits, all managed through Family Link.
details: Google Wallet has introduced a new feature allowing parents to create secure balances for their children and teens. This enables kids to use Google Pay for tap-to-pay transactions on NFC-enabled Android or Wear OS devices, providing financial independence without needing a bank account.

Parents maintain full control over these balances. They can set specific spending limits and monitor all transactions in real time. An instant lock/unlock feature is also available, offering peace of mind if a child's linked device is lost.

At launch, parents can transfer money directly from their accounts to the child's secure balance. Google has also announced that the ability to schedule automated regular payments will be rolled out soon. All aspects of this new functionality are managed through Google's Family Link parental control app.

This new secure balance feature complements existing Google Wallet functionalities for kids, which already include access to loyalty cards, gift cards, library cards, boarding passes, and event tickets.

With this update, Google Wallet is catching up to other solutions in the market. Android users previously relied on third-party apps like GoHenry and Greenlight for similar features, while Apple users have had access to Apple Cash Family for several years.

headline_marked: [[Hackers stalked WIRED reporter]] by hijacking a $30 kids' smartwatch, revealing major security flaws
headline: Hackers stalked WIRED reporter by hijacking a $30 kids' smartwatch, revealing major security flaws
summary: A security researcher demonstrated how easily a cheap child's smartwatch could be hijacked for silent tracking, photo, and audio capture. This vulnerability affects dozens of other brands using the same insecure backend platforms.
details: A WIRED reporter wore a $30 child's smartwatch that was easily hijacked by security researcher Vangelis Stykas. The device allowed silent tracking, photo, and audio capture without the wearer's knowledge or any indication on the watch itself.

Stykas demonstrated tracking the reporter's location via Wi-Fi network identifiers, even when GPS malfunctioned. He later used the watch to surreptitiously take photos as the reporter entered an elevator and sat at his desk, then recorded audio of a coworker's conversation.

The smartwatch, sold by an obscure company called CJC and manufactured by YiQingTeng Electronics, utilizes an online platform also used by dozens of other smartwatch brands. This widespread adoption suggests a broad vulnerability to similar digital stalking.

At the Black Hat cybersecurity conference, Stykas and Felipe Solferini will present their findings. They analyzed over 70 GPS-enabled watches and car accessories, discovering that more than 30 use technology from YiQingTeng (also Wonlex/SETracker) and another 30+ use NewGPS2012.

Combined with SinoTrack, these three supply chains account for tens of millions of GPS tracker gadgets. All three were found to have significant security flaws, including a lack of authentication, making children's watches vulnerable to tracking, location spoofing, message interception, and silent eavesdropping/capture.

The researchers also found server-side vulnerabilities that exposed consumer information, allowed code execution, and in one instance, suggested prior unauthorized access to the system's backend. Stykas warned that "millions of kids are being exposed and vulnerable to exploitation."
